intro: Six RO systems worth putting under a sink or on a counter, sorted by how they make water, how much they waste and what they certify to. The Waterdrop G3P800 is the pick for most kitchens.

Reverse osmosis is the one home filter type that removes almost everything dissolved in water, from lead and nitrate to the fluoride and PFAS that carbon struggles with. The catch is that RO systems vary far more than their marketing suggests: some fill a glass in eight seconds and some take a minute, some send four gallons down the drain for every one you drink, and some carry a real NSF/ANSI 58 certificate while others carry a logo. This guide sorts six systems on the specs that decide which one you will actually live with.
quickAnswer: the Waterdrop G3P800 Tankless Reverse Osmosis System is our #1 pick (best overall). The RO system to buy if you want fast, low-waste water and have an outlet under the sink.

Reverse osmosis is the finishing step for drinking and cooking water, not a whole-house solution. If you are still deciding what kind of filtration your home needs at all, start with our guide to the [best water filtration system for home](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/), which covers whole-house carbon, softeners and well treatment alongside RO. THE RULE
Buy for the drain ratio and the certificate, not the stage count.

A ten-stage system with a 1:4 drain ratio and no NSF/ANSI 58 certificate is worse than a four-stage system with a 2:1 ratio and a real certificate. Stage counts are marketing; the membrane and the paperwork are the product.

sections.h: How Reverse Osmosis Works, and What It Removes

blocks.p: A reverse osmosis membrane is a sheet of thin-film composite wound into a cartridge, with pores so small that water molecules pass and most dissolved salts, metals and larger organic molecules do not. Household water pressure pushes water across the membrane. Clean water, called permeate, comes out one side; the rejected minerals and contaminants leave in a continuous stream of concentrate that goes to the drain. That drain stream is not a defect. It is how the membrane keeps itself from clogging.

Because the membrane works on dissolved solids rather than adsorption, RO handles contaminants that carbon alone struggles with: nitrate, fluoride, arsenic, hexavalent chromium, many PFAS compounds and total dissolved solids generally. The carbon pre-filters in front of the membrane take out chlorine, which would otherwise attack the thin-film membrane, and the carbon post-filter catches any taste or odor that slips through. Sediment pre-filters protect everything downstream from grit.

What RO does not do is make unsafe water safe. Manufacturers say it plainly in their manuals: these systems are for use on water that is already microbiologically safe, such as municipal water or a tested well. A UV stage, like the one on the G3P800, adds a layer of protection, but it is not a substitute for proper well treatment. If you are on a private well with bacteria or high iron, fix that first at the point of entry and use RO as the drinking-water polish.

The single most useful thing you can do before buying is to know what is in your water. Municipal customers can read their utility's annual Consumer Confidence Report. Well owners should send a sample to a certified lab. If the report shows high nitrate, arsenic, fluoride you want gone, or PFAS, RO is the right tool. If it shows only chlorine taste, a carbon filter is cheaper, wastes no water, and will make you just as happy.

The table below puts the numbers that decide day-to-day life side by side. GPD is the membrane's rated production under the manufacturer's test conditions; your real output will be lower at lower pressure and in cold water. The drain ratio is purified water to concentrate where the maker publishes it. Certification is listed as the manufacturer or its retailers describe it, and we flag the one system certified through WQA rather than an NSF-standard lab.

Two patterns jump out. First, the tankless systems are dramatically more efficient. A pumped tankless unit runs the membrane at a consistent high pressure, which is what lets Waterdrop publish 2:1 and 3:1 ratios. Conventional tank systems run on line pressure that drops as the tank fills, and the back-pressure from the tank makes the membrane less efficient as it goes; that is why their makers tend not to publish a ratio at all, and why owners commonly report three to four gallons of concentrate per gallon of permeate.

Second, the tank systems win on simplicity and running cost. Nothing to plug in, nothing to fail electrically, and three of them use standard-size cartridges you can buy from any filter brand. If your sink cabinet has the room and your house has 50 psi or more, that is a perfectly good way to get RO water, and it is still how most RO systems in American kitchens work.

Treat the certification column as the most important one. NSF/ANSI 58 is the standard written specifically for reverse osmosis drinking water systems and covers structural integrity, materials safety and TDS reduction, plus any extra contaminant claims the maker chooses to certify. A system that claims to remove PFAS or lead should have those claims listed on its performance data sheet, which you can request from the manufacturer or find on the certifier's website.

Gallons per day is measured at a standard test pressure and temperature, typically around 60 psi and 77 F. Real kitchens are rarely that friendly. Cold winter water and 45 psi can cut a membrane's output by a third or more. On a tank system that mostly shows up as a slower refill. On a tankless system the pump compensates, which is one reason tankless ratings hold up better in use. For a tank system, a 50 or 75 GPD membrane is plenty for drinking and cooking; nobody needs 75 gallons a day of drinking water.

This is the number that shows up on your water bill. At 3:1, making a gallon of drinking water sends a third of a gallon to the drain. At 1:4, the same gallon costs four gallons of waste. For a family drinking and cooking with three gallons a day, that difference is roughly a thousand gallons a year on a typical tank system versus a few hundred on a high-efficiency tankless one. In drought-restricted areas, a published ratio of 2:1 or better is worth paying for.

Look for NSF/ANSI 58 from an accredited certifier: NSF itself, IAPMO R&T, or the Water Quality Association's Gold Seal program. Then look at what the certificate covers. Some systems are certified for TDS reduction only; others list lead, arsenic, nitrate, fluoride or PFOA/PFOS. Marketing that says a system is tested to NSF standards is not the same as certified. A certified system appears in the certifier's public database under the exact model number.

Check your house pressure before buying a tank system. A cheap gauge on an outdoor hose bib tells you in thirty seconds. Most tank systems want at least 40 to 45 psi; below that, output collapses and waste climbs. If your pressure is low, buy a pumped tankless system or add a permeate pump to a tank system. The Home Master's ERP version builds that pump in, and it needs no electricity.

Every under-sink RO needs its own dedicated faucet, which means either an existing sprayer hole, a soap dispenser hole you can repurpose, or drilling the countertop. Filter format matters for running cost: standard 10-inch housings accept generic cartridges, while quick-twist and modular systems tie you to the maker's cartridges in exchange for cleaner, faster changes.

sections.h: Tank vs Tankless vs Countertop RO

blocks.p: Tank systems are the traditional design. A slow membrane fills a pressurized storage tank, usually three to four gallons of usable water, and the faucet draws from it. Upsides: no power, low cost, cheap filters, and a reserve that still works during a power cut. Downsides: the tank eats half the sink cabinet, flow slows as it empties, waste is high, and stored water sitting in a tank can pick up a slight plastic or stale taste if the system is not used daily. A final carbon stage after the tank exists precisely to fix that.

Tankless systems put a pump in front of the membrane and make water on demand. They need a 120V outlet under the sink, and they make a quiet hum when running. In exchange, they fill a glass in seconds, never run out, take up roughly the footprint of a shoebox lying on its side, and waste much less water. They also tend to use proprietary twist-in cartridges, which are easier to change and more expensive to buy. For most kitchens with an outlet, tankless is now the better choice.

Countertop RO units, like the AquaTru, are batch systems. You fill a tank by hand, the unit filters it into a second tank, and you pour from that. They need no installation at all and are the only realistic RO option for most renters. The limits are capacity and convenience: three-quarters of a gallon goes fast, and refilling a tap tank several times a day gets old for a family. They also take up counter space you may not have to spare.

A simple way to decide: if you own the home and have an outlet under the sink, go tankless. If you own the home but adding an outlet is a hassle, go tank. If you rent, live alone or in a pair, or simply refuse to drill your countertop, go countertop. Water chemistry does not change the decision much, because all three use the same kind of thin-film membrane.

sections.h: Alkaline and Remineralization Stages: Worth It?

blocks.p: RO strips calcium, magnesium and bicarbonate along with the contaminants, and the result is water with very low TDS and a slightly acidic pH, usually somewhere around 6 to 6.5. It is perfectly safe to drink; the minerals you need come from food, not water. But many people find it tastes flat or faintly sour, especially if they are used to hard municipal water or spring water.

A remineralization stage adds a small amount of calcium and magnesium back after the membrane, raising pH and giving the water some body. Single-pass alkaline cartridges, like the one on the iSpring RCC7AK, make a noticeable difference. Home Master's two-pass design goes further, and its stated target of 30 to 60 mg/L of minerals lands the water in roughly the range of a mild spring water. If taste is why you are buying RO, this is the feature to pay attention to.

Be skeptical of health claims attached to alkaline water. The amount of mineral added is small, and stomach acid neutralizes any modest pH difference within seconds. Buy a remineralization stage because you prefer the taste, or because you want RO water that is a little less aggressive toward copper fittings and kettles, not because a listing promises antioxidant benefits.

If you already own a basic RO system and dislike the taste, you do not need to replace it. Inline remineralization cartridges are available for most standard systems and plug into the line between the post-carbon and the faucet. That is a cheap test of whether minerals fix the problem for you before you spend money on a different system.

Under-sink RO installation is a two-to-three hour job for a confident DIYer, and every system on this list ships with the parts. You tee into the cold supply line with a feed valve, clamp a drain saddle onto the sink drain above the trap, mount the faucet, run tubing, and either position the tank or mount the tankless unit. The steps that cause trouble are the faucet hole on stone or quartz countertops, which may need a diamond core bit or a professional, and getting the drain saddle positioned so concentrate does not back up.

Measure the cabinet before you order. A tank system needs room for a tank roughly 11 inches wide and 15 inches tall plus a filter manifold about 15 inches wide, and it all has to share space with the disposal, the trash can and the cleaning supplies. The G3P800 lists dimensions of about 18 by 6 by 18 inches, standing upright, with nothing else to place. If your disposal and drain plumbing already crowd the cabinet, tankless is often the only system that fits.

Tankless systems need power. If there is a disposal or dishwasher outlet under the sink, you are set; if not, adding a receptacle is a job for an electrician in most jurisdictions. Do not run an extension cord through the cabinet wall, and do not plug a pumped RO into a switched disposal outlet, because the unit will lose power every time the switch is off.

Some households also run an RO line to the refrigerator's water dispenser and ice maker. All of these systems can do it with a tee kit, but expect lower pressure at the fridge from a tank system, and check the fridge maker's minimum inlet pressure. Pumped tankless systems handle a fridge line better. Use PEX or the supplied polyethylene tubing; copper is not a good match for low-TDS RO water over the long term.

The purchase price is the smaller part of what an RO system costs over five years. Pre-filters typically need changing every six to twelve months, post-filters and remineralization cartridges about once a year, and the membrane every two to four years depending on water hardness and chlorine levels. Before you buy, price a year of filters for the exact model, and compare that figure across systems rather than the sticker price.

Standard 10-inch cartridges, used by the iSpring and APEC, are the cheapest route, with generic sets widely available. Quick-twist and modular formats, used by Waterdrop, Home Master and AquaTru, cost more per change but take seconds to swap and avoid wet hands and stuck housings. Which you prefer depends on whether money or convenience matters more. Either way, change them on schedule: a spent carbon pre-filter lets chlorine through, and chlorine destroys the membrane, which is the expensive part.

Watch the TDS number. A cheap handheld TDS meter, or the built-in readout on the G3P800 faucet, compares the tap water to the RO water. A healthy membrane removes the large majority of dissolved solids. When the rejection rate starts slipping noticeably, it is time for a new membrane, regardless of what the calendar says. This is the most reliable way to stop paying for filters you do not need yet, or drinking water from one that has quietly failed.

Do not forget the water itself. On a tank system wasting four gallons per gallon made, a household using three gallons a day sends thousands of gallons down the drain each year. On metered water, especially with sewer charges added, that cost is real, and it is the strongest financial argument for a tankless system with a published 2:1 or 3:1 ratio.

sections.h: Which Reverse Osmosis System Should You Buy?

blocks.p: **Most kitchens:** the Waterdrop G3P800. It is fast, efficient, compact and transparent about when it needs service. If the UV stage and the 3:1 ratio are not worth the premium to you, the G3P600 gives you most of the experience for less.

**No outlet, or a tight budget:** the iSpring RCC7AK. It needs no power, its filters are cheap and universal, and the alkaline stage softens the flat RO taste. The APEC ROES-50 is the plainer, cheaper alternative if you do not care about remineralization and just want reliable drinking and coffee water.

**Taste above all:** the Home Master TMAFC Artesian Full Contact. Its two-pass remineralization is the best fix for people who have tried RO and disliked it. Spend the extra on the ERP permeate-pump version if your water pressure is under 50 psi.

**Renters and small households:** the AquaTru Classic. No plumbing, the broadest certification list here, and it moves with you. For a family of four that cooks with filtered water, it will feel small; for one or two people, it is the easiest RO system to live with.

Whichever you choose, confirm the certification on the certifier's database, check your water pressure, and price a year of filters before you click buy. And if your water test shows problems throughout the house rather than just at the tap, revisit our [whole-home water filtration guide](/best-water-filtration-system-for-home/) first: an RO system at the sink cannot fix hard water in the shower or iron in the laundry.

mistakes: Buying RO when a carbon filter would do

If your water report shows only chlorine taste and odor, reverse osmosis is overkill. A good carbon block filter costs less, wastes no water and needs no drain connection. Save RO for nitrate, fluoride, arsenic, PFAS or high TDS, which carbon cannot reliably remove. Test first and buy the filter that matches what is actually in your water.
Ignoring water pressure on a tank system

Tank RO systems depend on line pressure. Below about 40 to 45 psi, output drops sharply, the tank never fills properly and the waste ratio gets worse. Check your pressure with a gauge on a hose bib before ordering. If it is low, buy a pumped tankless system or add a permeate pump rather than blaming the membrane later.

A ten-stage label often means two extra carbon cartridges and a mineral stage padded out with marketing. What matters is the membrane, the drain ratio and the certificate. Compare the NSF/ANSI 58 listing and the published efficiency, not the number of housings, and do not pay extra just because a system has more of them.

The carbon pre-filter is there to stop chlorine from reaching the membrane. Let it run past its life and chlorine breaks through, damaging the thin-film membrane, which is the costliest part of the system. Put the change dates in your calendar on install day and keep a spare set on the shelf so you are never tempted to stretch them.
Plugging a tankless unit into a switched outlet

Many sink cabinets have a single outlet controlled by the disposal switch. Plug a pumped RO into it and the system only works while the disposal switch is on. Use an always-on receptacle, have an electrician add one if needed, and never run an extension cord through the back of the cabinet.
bottomLine: Reverse osmosis is the most thorough drinking-water treatment you can put in a kitchen, and the modern tankless systems have fixed most of what people used to dislike about it: slow flow, cabinet clutter and wasted water. The Waterdrop G3P800 is the one to buy if you can give it an outlet. If you cannot, a well-certified tank system like the iSpring RCC7AK still does the job for less, and the AquaTru Classic brings RO to people who cannot touch the plumbing at all. Test your water first, confirm the certificate, and price a year of filters before you choose.

faqs.q: What is the best reverse osmosis system for home use?
faqs.a: For most homes with an outlet under the kitchen sink, the Waterdrop G3P800 is the best reverse osmosis system: 800 GPD, a 3:1 pure-to-drain ratio, NSF/ANSI 58 certification and a TDS faucet. Without an outlet, the iSpring RCC7AK is the best tank system. Renters should look at the AquaTru Classic countertop unit, which needs no plumbing.

faqs.q: Is tankless reverse osmosis better than a tank system?
faqs.a: For most kitchens, yes. Tankless systems make water on demand, so flow never tapers, they waste far less water thanks to a built-in pump, and they free up cabinet space. The trade-offs are that they need a 120V outlet under the sink and use proprietary filters that cost more. Tank systems remain the better choice where power is unavailable.

faqs.q: How much water does a reverse osmosis system waste?
faqs.a: It depends on the design. High-efficiency tankless systems publish ratios of 2:1 or 3:1, meaning one gallon of concentrate per two or three gallons of drinking water. Conventional tank systems running on line pressure commonly waste three to four gallons per gallon made. A permeate pump or higher feed pressure improves a tank system's ratio.

faqs.q: Does reverse osmosis remove fluoride and PFAS?
faqs.a: Reverse osmosis is one of the few home technologies that reliably reduces fluoride, and certified systems also reduce many PFAS compounds, including PFOA and PFOS. Check the system's performance data sheet for the specific claim, because certification covers only the contaminants listed. The AquaTru Classic, for example, lists P473 certification for PFOA and PFOS reduction.

faqs.q: Is reverse osmosis water bad for you because it removes minerals?
faqs.a: No. Reverse osmosis water is safe to drink, and the minerals your body needs come overwhelmingly from food rather than water. RO water can taste flat, which is why many systems add a remineralization stage. Choose one because you prefer the taste, not because RO water is unhealthy without it.

faqs.q: How often do you change reverse osmosis filters?
faqs.a: Pre-filters usually last six to twelve months, post-filters and mineral cartridges about a year, and the membrane two to four years, depending on water hardness and chlorine levels. The most reliable signal for the membrane is a TDS reading: when the RO water's TDS rises noticeably relative to the tap, the membrane is due.

faqs.q: Can I install a reverse osmosis system myself?
faqs.a: Yes, most people can install an under-sink RO system in two to three hours with basic tools. You connect a feed valve to the cold line, fit a drain saddle, mount the faucet and run tubing. Drilling a faucet hole through stone or quartz is the step most people hand to a pro. Countertop units like the AquaTru need no installation at all.
